summary: Describes four DHCPv6 options for Network Information Service configuration: NIS Servers, NIS+ Servers, NIS Client Domain Name and NIS+ Client Domain Name. They let a network hand this setup information to IPv6 clients automatically.

eli5.summary: When a computer joins a network, it needs to know which helper servers to use. This document adds ways for the network to tell it.

questions: what are the dhcpv6 nis options
how does dhcpv6 configure nis servers
subtitle: Four DHCPv6 options that tell IPv6 clients which NIS or NIS+ servers and domain names to use.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts that use the Network Information Service (NIS) or NIS+ need to know which servers to ask and which domain they belong to, and DHCPv6 had no way to hand that out.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four DHCPv6 options: NIS Servers (27), NIS+ Servers (28), NIS Client Domain Name (29) and NIS+ Client Domain Name (30). The server lists IPv6 addresses or a domain name in the option.
tldr.outcome: A client can learn its NIS or NIS+ setup automatically, but only for servers reachable over IPv6. An intruder DHCPv6 server could abuse the options, so clients SHOULD use authenticated DHCP.

today: RFC 3898 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the four DHCPv6 options for NIS and NIS+ configuration, built on RFC 3315.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3898 describes four options for passing configuration related to the Network Information Service (NIS) in DHCPv6, which is specified in RFC 3315.

The options can only configure information about NIS servers that can be reached using IPv6. The DHCP option for IPv4 NIS servers is found in RFC 2132. The RFC says mechanisms for dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 applications are being considered but are not specified here.
sections.eli5: Some computers look things up from a shared directory server. This note teaches the network to tell a new IPv6 computer where that directory is.

sections.title: The Two Server-List Options
sections.content:
The NIS Servers option (OPTION_NIS_SERVERS, code 27) and the NIS+ Servers option (OPTION_NISP_SERVERS, code 28) have the same layout: an option code, an option-len field, and then one or more IPv6 addresses, one per server.

option-len is the length of the server fields in octets and must be a multiple of 16, since each IPv6 address takes 16 octets. Clients MUST treat the list as ordered, and the server MAY list the servers in order of preference.
sections.eli5: It is a list of phone numbers for helper computers, written in the order you should try them.

sections.title: The Two Domain Name Options
sections.content:
The NIS Client Domain Name option (OPTION_NIS_DOMAIN_NAME, code 29) and the NIS+ Client Domain Name option (OPTION_NISP_DOMAIN_NAME, code 30) let the server tell the client which NIS or NIS+ domain name it should use.

Each carries an option-len and then the domain name (nis-domain-name or nisp-domain-name). The name MUST be encoded as the DHCPv6 specification describes in its section on the representation and use of domain names.
sections.eli5: This is the name of the group the computer belongs to, like the name of your school class, so it knows whose list to read.

sections.title: Where the Options Appear
sections.content:
The four options MUST NOT appear in any DHCPv6 message other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply.

A client MAY list the option numbers in the Option Request Option in these messages: Solicit, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reconfigure.
sections.eli5: There are only certain moments in the conversation when these notes may be passed, and the client can ask for them by number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An intruder DHCPv6 server could use these options to assign invalid NIS parameters, leaving clients unable to use NIS. It could also point clients at an intruder NIS or NIS+ server, and misdirected searches could be used to spoof NIS or NIS+ names.

The domain name options could make clients search invalid domains for incompletely specified names, with similar spoofing results. To avoid these attacks the DHCPv6 client SHOULD use authenticated DHCP.
sections.eli5: A trickster could hand out a fake card with the wrong phone numbers. Checking who gave you the card helps.

sections.title: IANA Option Codes
sections.content: IANA assigned the four option codes from the option-code space defined in the DHCPv6 specification: 27, 28, 29 and 30, described in sections 3 to 6 of the RFC.
sections.eli5: Each option got its own number in a big official list so everyone uses the same one.

items.label: OPTION_NIS_SERVERS
items.desc: List of IPv6 addresses of NIS servers.

items.label: OPTION_NISP_SERVERS
items.desc: List of IPv6 addresses of NIS+ servers.

items.label: OPTION_NIS_DOMAIN_NAME
items.desc: NIS domain name for the client.

items.label: OPTION_NISP_DOMAIN_NAME
items.desc: NIS+ domain name for the client.
